steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper ROG_PL on robust open-set node classification with graph neural networks when training labels contain both in-distribution and out-of-distribution noise. Motivate the problem and briefly describe the two parts of our method.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. GNNs and their assumptions (same distribution, large clean labeled data)
2. Open-set scenarios and noisy labels in practice
3. Why IND/OOD noise hurts: ambiguity problem
4. Need for robust open-set learning; gap in prior work
5. ROG PL: denoising + region-based open-set prototype learning

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. GNNs
- prominent for graph structured data: traffic state prediction, disease classification, user profile completion in social networks
- supervised GNN success rests on: train/test from identical distribution; large-scale reliable labeled data
- real world: such data usually unavailable

2. Open set + noise
- new-emerged OOD samples (not in any known class) prevalent
- outliers in training (OOD noise), open-set samples in testing
- clean labels need domain experts -> expensive, time-consuming
- cheaper: web search, crowdsourcing, user tags -> inevitably noisy

3. Harm
- OOD noise + IND noise (in-distribution, wrong labels) detrimental to GNNs
- ambiguity: intra-class variety (same label, different semantic categories); inter-class confusion (different intent classes, similar semantic categories)
- open-set unknown samples at test time complicate further

4. Gap
- need robust open-set models: learn from noisy data, classify known classes, identify unknown open-set samples
- prior work: robust learning or open-set learning separately; robust open-set with complex noise not sufficiently explored; harder for non-IID graph data

5. ROG PL (Fig. 1)
- step 1: denoising via label propagation; similarity-based pseudo-label propagation in latent space, remove low-confidence samples -> intra-class variety
- step 2: open-set prototypes per known class via non-overlapped regions; interior + border prototypes -> inter-class confusion
- iterative updates; classification loss + prototype diversity loss
- good performance on several benchmark graph datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are now a prominent technique for analyzing graph structured data in many real-world systems, for example traffic state prediction, disease classification, and completing user profiles in social networks. The recent success of supervised GNNs depends on two important cornerstones: the training and test data come from the same distribution, and there is large-scale, reliable, high-quality labeled data for training. But in real-world applications, large-scale labeled data from the same distribution as the test data is usually not available.

Real-world applications are normally open-set scenarios, so newly emerging out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, i.e. samples that are not in any known class, are common. If they show up in training they are outliers (OOD noise), and if they show up in testing they are open-set samples. Also, generating a clean labeled data set by hand would need domain experts to check the quality of the collected data, which is very expensive and takes a lot of time. Another option is to collect data and labels from web search, crowdsourcing and user tags. These data and labels are cheap, but they are inevitably noisy.

- Harm of noise:
  - OOD noise + IND noise (in-distribution, wrong labels) -> ambiguity problem
  - intra-class variety vs inter-class confusion
  - open-set unknowns at test time complicate it
- Gap:
  - need robust open-set models (learn from noise, classify known, identify unknown)
  - prior work separate; robust open-set with complex noise underexplored; harder for non-IID graphs
- ROG PL (Fig. 1):
  - denoising via similarity-based pseudo-label propagation, drop low-confidence samples
  - region-based open-set prototypes, interior + border prototypes
  - iterative, classification loss + prototype diversity loss
  - good results on benchmark graph datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are now a prominent technique for analyzing graph structured data in many real-world systems, for example traffic state prediction, disease classification, and completing user profiles in social networks. The recent success of supervised GNNs depends on two important cornerstones: the training and test data come from the same distribution, and there is large-scale, reliable, high-quality labeled data for training. But in real-world applications, large-scale labeled data from the same distribution as the test data is usually not available.

Real-world applications are normally open-set scenarios, so newly emerging out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, i.e. samples that are not in any known class, are common. If they show up in training they are outliers (OOD noise), and if they show up in testing they are open-set samples. Also, generating a clean labeled data set by hand would need domain experts to check the quality of the collected data, which is very expensive and takes a lot of time. Another option is to collect data and labels from web search, crowdsourcing and user tags. These data and labels are cheap, but they are inevitably noisy.

OOD noise and IND noise (in-distribution samples with wrong labels) can both be harmful to GNNs, because they cause the ambiguity problem. This includes the intra-class variety problem, where samples with the same class label can contain objects of different semantic categories, and the inter-class confusion problem, where samples of different intent classes can contain objects of similar semantic categories. On top of that, open-set unknown class samples appear at test time, which makes the problem even more complicated.

So we need to build robust open-set learning models that can learn from noisy data, classify the known class samples, and identify the unknown open-set class samples during testing. Previous works mostly looked at robust learning or open-set learning separately, and robust open-set learning with complex noise has not been explored enough so far. It is even harder for non-IID graph data.

In this paper we want to solve open-set graph learning with complex IND and OOD noise, as shown in Fig. 1, and we propose a new framework ROG PL for robust open-set node classification. It has two main steps: denoising using label propagation, and open-set prototype learning using regions. Specifically, in the latent representation space, ROG PL first fixes noisy labels with similarity-based pseudo-label propagation and removes low-confidence samples, which deals with the intra-class variety problem caused by noise. Then the second module learns open-set prototypes for each known class using non-overlapped regions and keeps both interior and border prototypes, to deal with the inter-class confusion problem. The two modules are updated iteratively under both a classification loss and a prototype diversity loss. Experiments with ROG PL on several benchmark graph datasets show that it performs well.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) [1,2,3,4] are now a prominent technique for analyzing graph structured data in many real-world systems, for example traffic state prediction [5], disease classification [6], and completing user profiles in social networks [7]. The recent success of supervised GNNs depends on two important cornerstones: the training and test data come from the same distribution, and there is large-scale, reliable, high-quality labeled data for training. But in real-world applications, large-scale labeled data from the same distribution as the test data is usually not available.

Real-world applications are normally open-set scenarios [8,9,10], so newly emerging out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, i.e. samples that are not in any known class, are common. If they show up in training they are outliers (OOD noise), and if they show up in testing they are open-set samples. Also, generating a clean labeled data set by hand would need domain experts to check the quality of the collected data, which is very expensive and takes a lot of time [11]. Another option is to collect data and labels from web search [12], crowdsourcing [13,14] and user tags [15,16]. These data and labels are cheap, but they are inevitably noisy [11,17].

OOD noise and IND noise (in-distribution samples with wrong labels) can both be harmful to GNNs [18], because they cause the ambiguity problem. This includes the intra-class variety problem, where samples with the same class label can contain objects of different semantic categories, and the inter-class confusion problem, where samples of different intent classes can contain objects of similar semantic categories [19]. On top of that, open-set unknown class samples appear at test time, which makes the problem even more complicated.

So we need to build robust open-set learning models [20] that can learn from noisy data, classify the known class samples, and identify the unknown open-set class samples during testing. Previous works mostly looked at robust learning or open-set learning separately, and robust open-set learning with complex noise has not been explored enough so far [21,22]. It is even harder for non-IID graph data.

In this paper we want to solve open-set graph learning with complex IND and OOD noise, as shown in Fig. 1, and we propose a new framework ROG PL for robust open-set node classification. It has two main steps: denoising using label propagation, and open-set prototype learning using regions. Specifically, in the latent representation space, ROG PL first fixes noisy labels with similarity-based pseudo-label propagation and removes low-confidence samples, which deals with the intra-class variety problem caused by noise. Then the second module learns open-set prototypes for each known class using non-overlapped regions and keeps both interior and border prototypes, to deal with the inter-class confusion problem. The two modules are updated iteratively under both a classification loss and a prototype diversity loss. Experiments with ROG PL on several benchmark graph datasets show that it performs well.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) [1,2,3,4] have become a prominent technique for analyzing graph structured data in many real-world systems, such as traffic state prediction [5], disease classification [6], and user profile completion in social networks [7]. The recent success of supervised GNNs rests on two crucial cornerstones: that the training and test data are drawn from an identical distribution, and that large-scale, reliable, high-quality labeled data are available for training. In real-world applications, however, large-scale labeled data drawn from the same distribution as the test data are usually unavailable.

Real-world applications are normally open-set scenarios [8,9,10], where newly emerged out-of-distribution (OOD) samples, i.e. samples that do not belong to any known class, are prevalent. They are outliers if they occur in training (OOD noise), and open-set samples if they occur in testing. Moreover, manually generating a clean labeled data set would involve domain experts evaluating the quality of the collected data, and is thus very expensive and time-consuming [11]. Alternatively, data and labels can be collected via web search [12], crowdsourcing [13,14] and user tags [15,16]. Such data and labels are cheap but inevitably noisy [11,17].

The presence of OOD noise and IND noise (in-distribution samples with incorrect labels) can be detrimental to GNNs [18], as they cause the ambiguity problem, including the intra-class variety problem, in which samples with the same class label may contain objects of different semantic categories, and the inter-class confusion problem, in which samples of different intent classes may contain objects of similar semantic categories [19]. Open-set unknown class samples occurring during testing further complicate this problem.

It is thus necessary to build robust open-set learning models [20] that can learn from noisy data, classifying known class samples and identifying unknown open-set class samples during testing. Previous works mainly focused on robust learning or open-set learning separately; the problem of robust open-set learning with complex noise has not been sufficiently explored so far [21,22], and it becomes even more difficult for non-IID graph data.

In this paper, as shown in Fig. 1, we propose a new framework, ROG PL, for robust open-set node classification, to solve the problem of open-set graph learning with complex IND and OOD noise. It consists of two main steps: denoising via label propagation, and open-set prototype learning via regions. Specifically, in the latent representation space, ROG PL first corrects noisy labels through similarity-based pseudo-label propagation and removes low-confidence samples, addressing the intra-class variety problem caused by noise. The second module then learns open-set prototypes for each known class via non-overlapped regions and retains both interior and border prototypes to remedy the inter-class confusion problem. The two modules are iteratively updated under the constraints of both a classification loss and a prototype diversity loss. Experimental evaluations of ROG PL on several benchmark graph datasets demonstrate its good performance.
